newsitem.title: USA: U.S. expected to give more food aid to N. Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. expected to give more food aid to N. Korea.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday was considering more food aid for North Korea following a new appeal by the U.N. World Food Programme, and officials said another American contribution was all but certain.
Washington has responded positively to all previous WFP appeals and "we're going to give this very serious consideration," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing.
"We are the largest contributor, and I would argue, the strongest supporter of the World Food Program's activities in North Korea," he said.
Other officials have said privately that they expect another U.S. contribution to be approved.

Although not directly linked to Washington's efforts to initiate peace talks between North Korea and its arch rival South Korea, U.S. officials acknowledge privately that treating Pyongyang's food crisis seriously is an important element in building trust with the Stalinist regime and persuading it to come to the negotiating table.
Burns said there was "some degree of urgency" to the food shortages faced by North Korea's Stalinist regime, and a formal U.S. response to the WFP appeal was expected shortly.
The WFP earlier on Wednesday launched an appeal for an additional $46 million in food aid to boost supplies the United Nations is sending for some 2.6 million children younger than 6.
Catherine Bertini, the head of the programme, told reporters tens of thousands of North Korean children are "wasting away" from malnutrition and many seem doomed to die.
Although this year's rice harvest was shaping up well, it could not provide enough for the Communist state to feed its 24 million people without continuing outside help, she said.

Bertini said her appeal, covering about 130,000 tonnes of food, was in addition to a $96 million appeal for 206,000 tonnes earlier this year that had been covered by donor governments and organisations.
But even with announced pledges and commercial barter imports, she added, North Korea still faced a food deficit of about 1 million tonnes this year.
The United States this year has given the WFP $25 million in response to earlier appeals for North Korea.
Burns said U.S. experts would evaluate the WFP request -- which officials have expected for the past month -- and make a recommendation to Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

North Korean officials, whose country long followed a philosophy of self-reliance and had few contacts with the non-Communist world, insist the food problem is entirely due to devastating floods and storms over the past three years.

But many analysts say the natural disasters, which hit at harvest time, have only compounded a steady decline in the rigidly state-controlled economy where major resources are poured into maintaining a powerful military machine.
